newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky says Albanian parties seek June 29 vote.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky says Albanian parties seek June 29 vote.

text.p: International mediator Franz Vranitzky said on Thursday that Albanian political parties had agreed they wanted elections to be held on June 29 but remained divided on the procedure for the vote.
"I think that we have achieved some progress today," Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), told reporters.
"I have listened to several parties and the government and they are all of the opinion that the elections should take place on June 29," he said.
Although the parties, which are united in an all-party emergency government, had not yet agreed on the conditions for the vote, Vranitzky said they were working to narrow the gaps.

"We cannot expect that within a few hours there are binding agreements," he said on his way out of lunch with Tritan Shehu, chairman of President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, and Fatos Nano, chairman of the Socialist Party.

The Socialists were the main opposition until the unity government was formed a month ago at the height of unrest sparked by the collapse of get-rich-quick savings schemes. The violence has claimed nearly 300 lives.
But Vranitzky added: "I think it was very important that the exponents of Albanian parties agreed they should try everything to find a consensus which is necessary to have a basis for the election."

Vranitzky diplomatically cancelled plans to visit the port of Vlore in the rebel-controlled south after tough talks with Berisha on Wednesday at which the president told him the elections could not go ahead if rebels remained in command.

Vranitzky, who said on Wednesday that he feared the elections were "in some way imperilled" because of differences between parties on how to deal with the rebels, said he had been told Vlore was "not entirely safe".
He said he also thought it was more important to stay in Tirana and press on with talks on the elections.
Parties remained divided over how they viewed the self-proclaimed rebel "committees of national salvation".
"That is certainly the hardest part about the whole election process," Vranitzky said.
He urged the government and rebels on Wednesday to hold "at least a minimum of dialogue" to unblock the situation. Berisha refused: "We are not negotiating with them. No."
Parties are also split on whether the system of electing 120 of parliament's 140 seats by a majority vote and the rest by proportional representation should be kept or changed.

The Democratic Party wants no change to the system that returned Berisha to power with a landslide victory last May. The elections were boycotted by the opposition and international observers reported widespread irregularities.
Justice Minister Spartak Ngjela said on Wednesday he wanted a switch to proportional representation.
Vranitzky said it was realistic not to insist on disarmament before the election. Albania is awash with guns after looting of depots left unmanned when soldiers and police deserted their posts.

"They (the parties) prefer to have the election at the fixed date rather than trying to collect the weapons without any time frame," he said. "I think it's a wise decision...It's a pragmatic decision."
